design_detail: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover in 9 men with previous recreational MDMA experience, run as outpatients. Each session lasted two days: 100 mg MDMA on day 1 and a second 100 mg dose 24 hours later, or matching placebo on both days, with at least a week between the two sessions. Physiological measures, psychomotor performance, 21 visual analogue scales, the Addiction Research Center Inventory, plasma cortisol and prolactin, and plasma and urine concentrations of MDMA and its metabolite MDA were measured repeatedly for 24 hours after each dose, with further plasma samples at 30 and 48 hours and urine to 72 hours. Peak effects and 6-hour areas under the curve were compared by two-way repeated-measures analysis of variance with drug condition and administration (first or second) as factors, with Tukey post-hoc tests and a three-way analysis including time.
can_establish: How the acute effects and plasma concentrations of a second 100 mg dose of MDMA taken 24 hours after a first compare with the first, within the same people against their own placebo days, under double-blind conditions.
cannot_establish: What happens at the intervals people actually use (the authors say 2-8 hours is the recreational pattern and that extrapolation to shorter intervals is difficult), after more than two doses, at larger doses, in women (none were studied), or over repeated weekends; and whether the smaller-than-expected effects reflect tolerance rather than ceiling effects on the rating scales and on pupil diameter, which the authors raise as an alternative.

sample.recruitment: Men recruited by word of mouth; the study was run at a municipal medical research institute in Barcelona (Materials and methods > Volunteers, p. 365).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Recreational use of MDMA on at least five previous occasions; medical screening by physician interview, physical examination, laboratory tests, urinalysis and electrocardiogram; psychiatric screening by structured DSM-IV interview excluding schizophrenia, psychosis and major affective disorder. Ten men were enrolled and one was excluded because his dextromethorphan phenotyping showed he was not an extensive metabolizer of the enzyme that clears MDMA, leaving nine (p. 365).
sample.demographics: Nine men, mean age 23 years (range 21-33), mean weight 73.3 kg (range 60.6-86.5), mean height 177 cm (range 168-189), with an average of 26 previous MDMA experiences (range 6-100). All but two smoked tobacco; all had used other stimulants, cannabis or hallucinogens; none met DSM-IV criteria for abuse or dependence other than nicotine, and none had a history of adverse reactions to MDMA (p. 365).
sample.attrition: No dropouts after enrolment; the one excluded participant was removed before the sessions on the basis of enzyme phenotyping.
sample.selection_effects: Men only, young, healthy, experienced with MDMA and screened to be fast metabolizers of it; people who metabolize MDMA slowly, who are the group most exposed to accumulation, were deliberately excluded, and women were not studied.

exposure.measurement: Drug given in the laboratory in identical opaque capsules and measured directly: plasma and urine MDMA and MDA by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry, sampled at baseline, 20, 40, 60 and 90 minutes and 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 10 and 24 hours after each dose, plus 30 and 48 hours after the second, with urine collected in four intervals to 24 hours and again to 72 hours (pp. 365-366).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: oral racemic MDMA 100 mg on day 1 followed by oral racemic MDMA 100 mg 24 hours later, or placebo on both days, supplied by the Spanish Ministry of Health and prepared by the institution's pharmacy (p. 365).
exposure.polysubstance: Participants were asked to refrain from any drug for two weeks before and during the study, with urine screening for opiates, cocaine metabolite, amphetamines and cannabinoids before each session; smoking was allowed only from 6 hours after dosing, and the paper attributes part of the late heart-rate rise in all conditions to smoking and meals (pp. 365-367).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Overnight fast and drug-free urine screen before each session day; at least one week between the two two-day sessions. At the 24-hour point most participants still had measurable MDMA in plasma from the first dose, averaging 12 ng/mL (p. 370).

comparison.controls: The same men in a placebo-placebo session, with each active day compared against its own temporal placebo (first dose against first placebo, second against second); the first and second placebo days were also compared with each other and differed only at three isolated time points on two performance measures.
comparison.matching: Within-person, randomized, double-blind crossover with at least a week between sessions.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable: every comparison is within person against the same person's placebo session.

outcomes.instruments: Systolic and diastolic blood pressure, heart rate, oral temperature and pupil diameter (Haab gauge) at 13 time points to 24 hours; simple reaction time, digit-symbol substitution and the Maddox-wing measure of extraocular balance; 21 visual analogue scales and the 49-item short-form Addiction Research Center Inventory with its five subscales; plasma cortisol and prolactin by immunoassay to 6 hours (pp. 365-366).
outcomes.validity_norms: Standard human-pharmacology battery used by this laboratory in earlier MDMA studies; the visual analogue scales have no external norms and the questionnaire subscales are validated in Spanish.
outcomes.operationalization: Acute tolerance is not formally defined or tested: the authors infer 'some degree of tolerance' where effects after the second dose were similar to the first despite higher plasma concentrations, and the absence of sensitization where no effect exceeded what the concentration predicted.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None at the family level: every variable was tested on three parameters (peak, 6-hour area under the curve, and the time course), with Tukey post-hoc comparisons at each time point, at p<0.05 (p. 366).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Double-blind with identical capsules; blinding integrity was not assessed, and 100 mg of MDMA in men with an average of 26 previous experiences is likely to have been recognizable.

analysis.effect_sizes: Effects are reported as F values with p values in Table 1 and as peak changes in the text; standardized effect sizes are not given. Pharmacokinetics (Table 2, n=9): MDMA area under the curve 1452 (SD 771) ng.h/mL after the first dose and 2564 (SD 762) after the second, a ratio of 1.77 (+77%, p<=0.001); peak concentration 180 (SD 33) and 232 (SD 39) ng/mL, a ratio of 1.29 (+29%, p<=0.001); elimination half-life 7.0 h (SD 2.2) and 8.8 h (SD 1.5); elimination constant 0.112 (SD 0.054) and 0.081 (SD 0.017) per hour. For the metabolite MDA: area under the curve 157 (SD 55) and 259 (SD 81), ratio 1.64 (+64%); peak 11 (SD 3) and 15 (SD 4) ng/mL, ratio 1.40 (+40%). Physiological peaks: systolic pressure +25 mm Hg after the first dose and +34 after the second; diastolic +10 and +20; heart rate +16 and +22 beats/min. Cortisol peak 14.11 against 21.08 microgram/mL, about 49% higher, with the area under the curve about 75% higher.
analysis.covariates: None; effects were expressed as change from each day's baseline before analysis.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration is mentioned. The study was approved by the local institutional review board and authorized by the Spanish Ministry of Health (number 98/112), and conformed to Spanish clinical-trial law (pp. 364-365, 375).
analysis.selective_reporting: Table 1 lists only the variables that reached significance somewhere, so the number of scales tested and found null can only be inferred; the Addiction Research Center Inventory and visual analogue time courses appear in figures without printed values.
analysis.power: No sample-size calculation. The authors state in their limitations that nine participants may not have had enough power to show differences in some variables, and that several questionnaire scales were near their ceiling.

interpretation_gap.results_show: A second 100 mg dose 24 hours after the first produced plasma concentrations far above simple accumulation (area under the curve 77% higher, peak 29% higher) and effects that were slightly larger than after the first dose on blood pressure, some subjective scales and cortisol, but smaller than those concentrations would predict; on pupil diameter, the Maddox-wing measure, one questionnaire subscale and prolactin the second dose produced the same response as the first. Hypertensive episodes (above 140 mm Hg systolic) occurred in 6 of 9 men after the first dose and 8 of 9 after the second, lasting on average 1 h against 1.4 h, and the two episodes of sinus tachycardia both followed the second dose.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that effects after the second administration were higher than after the first but lower than expected, and attributes the concentration rise to metabolic inhibition lasting at least 24 hours; the discussion says the unchanged responses suggest 'the possible appearance of some degree of tolerance'. This is appropriately hedged. The weaker point is that the tolerance reading rests on comparing an effect with an expectation that is not modelled: no concentration-effect relation is fitted, so 'lower than expected' is a judgement rather than a measurement, and the authors' own alternative explanation (ceiling effects on the scales and on pupil diameter) is not ruled out.

timeline.event: The same group, 50 mg then 100 mg two hours apart in 10 men: concentrations above dose proportionality again, with heart rate and the wanted subjective effects lower than the concentrations predicted
Two 100 mg doses 4 hours apart (Farre et al., 2015): peak concentrations roughly doubled while the two effect-time profiles were very similar
A 60 mg booster 2 hours after 120 mg: 1.5-fold higher peak concentration, effects prolonged by about an hour, peak effects unchanged

replication.where_it_stands: The finding that a second dose raises concentrations more than simple accumulation predicts, while effects rise less than concentrations do, has now been reproduced at 24-hour, 4-hour and 2-hour intervals and with a booster design, by two independent groups. The specific 24-hour finding rests on this study alone.

funding.funder: Grants from the Generalitat de Catalunya (2001SGR00407) and the Fondo de Investigacion Sanitaria (98/0181 and 01/1336) (p. 375).
funding.declared_conflicts: Not reported: the article carries no conflict-of-interest statement.
funding.affiliations_note: Institut Municipal d'Investigacio Medica and two Barcelona universities; the same group published the 2-hour-interval study (Peiro et al., 2013) and the 4-hour-interval study, so those are not independent replications of each other.

what_would_settle_it: A dose-ranging repeated-dose study that fits a concentration-effect model for each measure, so that 'lower than expected' becomes a measured shift in the concentration-response curve rather than a judgement; including women, people who metabolize MDMA slowly, intervals of 2-8 hours and scales without ceiling effects.

domains.domain: Randomization process (order of the two sessions)
domains.note: Described as randomized and crossover, but sequence generation and allocation concealment are not described and no period effect is reported.
At least one week between sessions, which is many half-lives, and the two placebo days behaved alike except at three isolated time points on two measures.
Double-blind with identical capsules, but blinding integrity was not tested and the active condition produced unmistakable effects in men with substantial previous MDMA experience.
All nine men completed both sessions; the one exclusion happened before dosing, on the basis of enzyme phenotyping.

Cardiovascular measures, pupil diameter, hormones and plasma concentrations are objective; the subjective scales that carry much of the tolerance argument are self-reports whose blinding cannot be assumed, and the authors state several were near their ceiling.
No protocol or pre-specified primary outcome; about forty outcomes tested on three parameters each without family-level correction; Table 1 shows only variables that reached significance somewhere.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: This is a well-run within-person, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover with objective pharmacokinetic measurement and matched placebo days, and the pharmacokinetic finding is internally strong (paired tests, p<=0.001, consistent in plasma and urine). The concerns are the untested blind, the number of uncorrected comparisons, and that the tolerance interpretation compares effects with an unmodelled expectation. The source can be cited for the size of the concentration rise after a second dose 24 hours later, for the direction of the cardiovascular and subjective changes, and for the observation that some measures did not increase; it cannot be cited for the size of any tolerance, for shorter intervals, for more than two doses, or for women.

key_findings.finding: A second 100 mg dose 24 hours after the first produced plasma concentrations well above simple accumulation: area under the curve 2564 ng.h/mL (SD 762) against 1452 (SD 771), a ratio of 1.77 (77% higher), and peak concentration 232 ng/mL (SD 39) against 180 (SD 33), a ratio of 1.29 (29% higher); both paired comparisons at p<=0.001. The elimination constant fell (0.112 to 0.081 per hour) and the half-life rose (7.0 h, SD 2.2, to 8.8 h, SD 1.5).
key_findings.locator: Table 2, MDMA rows; Results > Pharmacokinetics, 2nd paragraph (p. 370)

key_findings.finding: The metabolite MDA rose in parallel: area under the curve 259 ng.h/mL (SD 81) against 157 (SD 55), a ratio of 1.64 (64% higher), and peak 15 ng/mL (SD 4) against 11 (SD 3), a ratio of 1.40 (40% higher), both p<=0.001; urinary recoveries of both compounds were also higher after the second dose.
key_findings.locator: Table 2, MDA rows; Results > Pharmacokinetics, last paragraph (p. 370)

key_findings.finding: At the 24-hour point, just before the second dose, most participants still had measurable MDMA in plasma, averaging 12 ng/mL.

Blood pressure rose more after the second dose: the peak increase in systolic pressure was 34 mm Hg against 25 after the first dose, and in diastolic pressure 20 against 10; the differences were significant only at some time points in the first 2 hours. Heart rate rose 22 beats/min against 16, significant only at 40 minutes.
key_findings.locator: Results > Pharmacological effects, the paragraph beginning 'In reference to physiological parameters' (p. 367, right column); Figure 1 (p. 368)

key_findings.finding: Cardiovascular incidents were more common after the second dose: systolic pressure above 140 mm Hg was reached by 6 of 9 men after the first dose and 8 of 9 after the second, with mean episode duration 1 h (range 0.5-2) against 1.4 h (range 0.5-3); two men met criteria for sinus tachycardia (above 100 beats/min), both after the second dose, lasting 15-30 minutes.
key_findings.locator: Results > Pharmacological effects, the paragraph beginning 'In reference to physiological parameters' (p. 367, right column)

key_findings.finding: Subjective effects were slightly larger after the second dose, but significantly so on few scales: 'stimulated' (peak, area under the curve and time course), 'high', 'any effect', 'changes in lights', 'changes in hearing' and four questionnaire subscales, mostly on the time course rather than the peak. No hallucinations or psychotic symptoms occurred after either dose.
key_findings.locator: Results > Pharmacological effects, the paragraph beginning 'Subjective effects after administrations' (p. 370, left column); Table 1 (pp. 368-369); Figures 3-4 (pp. 371-372)

key_findings.finding: Several measures did not increase at all with the second dose despite the higher concentrations: pupil diameter, the Maddox-wing measure of extraocular balance, the amphetamine subscale of the questionnaire and plasma prolactin. Cortisol, by contrast, rose further: peak 21.08 against 14.11 microgram/mL, about 49% higher, with the area under the curve about 75% higher.
key_findings.locator: Results > Pharmacological effects, the paragraph on pupil diameter (p. 367) and the paragraph beginning 'Plasma hormone concentrations' (p. 370); Discussion, the paragraph beginning 'The pharmacological effects after the second administration' (p. 373)

key_findings.finding: The authors calculate that if the first dose's residual exposure is subtracted, the expected rise in area under the curve would be 39%, against the 77% observed, which they attribute to inhibition of MDMA's own metabolism lasting at least 24 hours.

Psychomotor performance did not differ between the two doses: both slightly reduced the number of digit-symbol responses and both produced similar extraocular tension, with no effect on reaction time.
key_findings.locator: Results > Pharmacological effects, the paragraph beginning 'Psychomotor performance results' (p. 370, left column); Figure 2 (p. 369)

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 prints a standard deviation beneath each median time to peak concentration (2 h with 0.26 for the first dose, 25.5 h with 0.33 for the second; 4 h with 6.88 and 28 h with 2.71 for the metabolite), although the legend and methods state that the time to peak was analysed by a rank test and reported as a median.
reporting_issues.consequence: A standard deviation around a median cannot be interpreted, and for the metabolite the value (6.88) is larger than the median itself (4 h); these dispersion figures should not be quoted.

reporting_issues.issue: The printed ratios do not all follow from the printed means: the metabolite's peak ratio is given as 1.40 (40%) while the rounded means (15 and 11 ng/mL) give 1.36, and the elimination half-life rises from 7.0 to 8.8 hours without a significance marker although the elimination constant it is derived from is discussed as having decreased.
reporting_issues.consequence: The ratios are presumably computed from unrounded individual values; a claim should cite the ratio with its significance marker rather than recomputing from the rounded table means, and should not describe the half-life change as significant.

reporting_issues.issue: Times to peak concentration are given from the start of the session rather than from each dose (2 h and 25.5 h; 4 h and 28 h for the metabolite), which the table does not state.
reporting_issues.consequence: Read as time since the second dose, the second-dose peak is at 1.5 hours, slightly earlier than the first dose's 2 hours; a reader taking 25.5 h at face value would misreport the time course.

reporting_issues.issue: The discussion lists the subjective scales that differed between doses as including 'changes in lights and sounds, changes in hearing', while the results list 'changes in lights' (peak and time course) and 'changes in hearing' (time course); there is no separate 'sounds' scale among the 21 listed in the methods.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor wording drift between results and discussion; the results list and Table 1 should be used.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 includes only variables that reached significance in at least one comparison, so the denominator for the subjective findings (21 visual analogue scales and five questionnaire subscales, each tested on three parameters) is not visible in the table.
reporting_issues.consequence: The number of comparisons behind the handful of significant subjective differences is larger than the table suggests, and the paper applies no family-level correction.

reporting_issues.issue: The study's central interpretation, that effects were lower than expected given the concentrations, is not supported by a fitted concentration-effect relation; the authors note in their own limitations that ceiling effects on the questionnaire scales and on pupil diameter could produce the same pattern.
reporting_issues.consequence: The claim of acute tolerance from this study should be stated as an unchanged or slightly increased response despite higher concentrations, with the ceiling-effect alternative named.

verification.source_read: PDF pp. 364-375 (PDFs/MDMA/Farre_2004_RepeatedDosesPharmacology.pdf), full text; Table 2 (p. 370) is printed sideways and was read from a rotated render of the page, and Table 1 (pp. 368-369) was read in the extracted text and checked against the page images.
